noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know that alkanes are used as fuels and obtained from the fractional distillation, cracking and reforming of crude oil, and be able to write equations for these reactions

primer.text: Crude oil leaves the well as a mixture worth nothing until it is sorted and reshaped. This note follows the refinery path: fractional distillation dividing fractions by boiling point, cracking splitting heavy chains into light alkenes, and reforming straight chains into branched and cyclic isomers that burn more cleanly.

lessons.title: Fractional distillation and reforming
lessons.opening: Crude oil arrives as a jumble of chain lengths worth little until the refinery sorts it. Fractional distillation divides fractions by boiling point, and reforming then reshapes straight chains into branched and cyclic isomers that burn more cleanly in engines.
keyPoints: Crude oil is heated and its vapours rise up a fractionating column, condensing at different heights.
Fractions separate because each boiling-point band collects at its own level of the column.
Shorter chains condense near the cool top; longer chains condense near the hot bottom.
Reforming converts straight-chain alkanes into branched and cyclic isomers.
Reformed fuels burn more efficiently, which is why refiners pay to reshape their chains.

low.restatement: Heat the oil, let the vapours climb a tower: long chains fall out low where it is hot, short chains climb higher before condensing, and each level drains one fraction.
low.analogy: A running race up a spiral staircase where heavier runners (long chains) drop out on the first floors and light ones (short chains) reach the top.
low.examPointer: Link boiling point to chain length explicitly - questions reward the causal chain, not just 'they separate'.

medium.restatement: Reforming adds ring strain and branching: cyclohexane from hexane releases hydrogen (CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3 -> C6H12 + H2), and branched isomers resist engine knocking better than straight chains.
medium.analogy: Reforming is tailoring the same cloth (same atoms) into a better-fitting garment (burning pattern) for the engine.
medium.examPointer: When writing reforming equations, balance the hydrogen gas released - the ring closure costs two hydrogens that appear as H2.

check.stem: How does a fractionating column separate crude oil?

options.text: Vapours condense at different heights according to boiling point
options.explanation: Each fraction condenses where the column temperature matches its boiling band.

options.text: A filter catches the largest molecules
options.explanation: Separation is by condensation, not filtration.
No chemistry runs in the column - it is physical separation.
No spinning occurs in the column.

check.stem: Where do the longest-chain fractions condense in the column?

options.explanation: Long chains boil high, so they condense first, low down.
That is where short-chain gases collect.
The temperature gradient sorts them, so they concentrate.
Condensation happens inside.

check.stem: What does reforming do to straight-chain alkanes?

options.text: Converts them into branched and cyclic isomers
options.explanation: Same atoms, better burning shape.

options.text: Cracks them into two smaller chains
options.explanation: That is cracking's job.
Reforming actually releases hydrogen.
Desulfurisation is a separate cleanup.

check.stem: Which equation represents the reforming of hexane into cyclohexane?

options.explanation: Ring closure releases the two hydrogens as hydrogen gas.
Cyclohexane holds 12 hydrogens, not 14.
That is full aromatisation beyond this scope.
Reforming consumes no oxygen.

check.stem: Why do engines burn branched and cyclic alkanes more efficiently?

options.explanation: Branching steadies the combustion front.

options.text: They contain more energy per gram
options.explanation: The energy content barely changes with branching.

options.text: They are more volatile than any straight chain
options.explanation: Volatility is not the efficiency mechanism cited.
They are pure hydrocarbons.

check.stem: Describe how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions.
check.modelAnswer: Heat the crude oil, send the vapours up a fractionating column, and collect each fraction where it condenses according to its boiling-point band.

check.stem: State the purpose of reforming in the refinery.
check.modelAnswer: Reforming reshapes straight-chain alkanes into branched and cyclic isomers that burn more cleanly and efficiently in engines.

check.stem: Explain why fractional distillation works at all - what property drives the separation?
check.modelAnswer: Longer alkane chains exert stronger intermolecular forces, raising their boiling points, so each chain length condenses at the column height whose temperature matches that boiling point.

check.stem: Hexane reformed to cyclohexane releases hydrogen gas. Show that the hydrogen count balances in CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3 -> C6H12 + H2.
check.modelAnswer: Hexane carries 14 hydrogens; cyclohexane holds 12 and the released H2 carries 2, so 14 = 12 + 2 and the ledger closes.

lessons.title: Cracking the heavy fractions
lessons.opening: Long chains are abundant and low-demand; short alkenes are scarce and precious. Cracking rebalances the market by splitting heavy fractions under heat and catalyst into smaller alkanes plus alkenes - the one refinery reaction that creates unsaturation.
keyPoints: Cracking splits long-chain alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes using heat and a catalyst.
The demand for short alkenes drives the economics: cracking manufactures them from surplus heavy fractions.
A typical split is decane to octane plus ethene: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4.
Both product families must balance against the parent chain's carbon and hydrogen counts.
Cracking is the opposite of polymerisation in spirit: it breaks chains rather than building them.

low.restatement: Heat a heavy alkane over a catalyst and it snaps into a shorter alkane plus an alkene; check your answer by counting carbons and hydrogens on both sides.
low.analogy: A long train splits into a short train and a carriage that can couple with others (the alkene's open bond).
low.examPointer: Always verify a cracking equation with an atom count - an unbalanced hydrogen ledger is the commonest examiner deduction.

medium.restatement: The catalysed route trades C-C single bonds for a new C=C pi bond, so the hydrogen redistribution must satisfy both the alkane product and the alkene product simultaneously - one equation, two ledgers.
medium.analogy: Cutting one rope into two pieces whose combined length equals the original - the alkene piece carries the frayed end (the pi bond).
medium.examPointer: State the catalyst (aluminium oxide or zeolite) when the question asks for conditions, alongside the heat.

check.stem: What are the products of cracking a long alkane?

options.text: A shorter alkane and an alkene
options.explanation: The split always creates one unsaturated piece.
That would lose the unsaturation chemistry cracking exists to create.
The saturated remainder stays an alkane.
No combustion occurs in cracking.

options.text: Heat plus a catalyst such as aluminium oxide
options.explanation: Thermal catalytic cracking is the standard route.

options.text: A nickel catalyst at room temperature
options.explanation: Nickel serves hydrogenation.
UV starts radical substitution, not chain splitting.
Cold steam splits nothing.

check.stem: Check the cracking equation C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4. Is it balanced?

options.explanation: Both ledgers close.

options.text: No: the hydrogens do not match
options.explanation: 18 + 4 = 22 - they do match.

options.text: No: the carbons do not match
options.explanation: 8 + 2 = 10 - they do match.

options.text: It cannot be checked without coefficients
options.explanation: The coefficient 1 throughout makes the check direct.

check.stem: Why do refineries crack heavy fractions rather than selling them as-is?

options.text: Short-chain alkenes are in high demand and heavy fractions are surplus
options.explanation: Cracking converts surplus into wanted feedstock.
Toxicity is not the cracking driver.
They burn, just less usefully in engines.
Desulfurisation is a separate process.

check.stem: Which statement links cracking to polymerisation?

options.text: Cracking breaks chains and creates alkenes; polymerisation consumes alkene double bonds to build chains
options.explanation: The two processes reverse each other.
Cracking creates pi bonds; polymerisation opens them.
Cracking's signature conditions are heat and catalyst.
Cracking produces small molecules.

check.stem: Define cracking and name the catalyst family used.
check.modelAnswer: Cracking splits long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes, using heat and a catalyst such as aluminium oxide or zeolite.

check.stem: Write a balanced equation for cracking decane into octane and ethene.
check.modelAnswer: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4, balanced with carbons 10 = 8 + 2 and hydrogens 22 = 18 + 4.

check.stem: Explain why cracking increases the value of a barrel of crude oil.
check.modelAnswer: The heavy fraction is abundant and low-priced, while the small alkene molecules it yields are versatile feedstock for polymers and alcohols, so splitting heavy chains converts surplus stock into premium products.

check.stem: A student proposes the cracking equation C8H18 -> C6H14 + C2H6. Check it and state the verdict.
check.modelAnswer: The carbons balance (8 = 6 + 2) but the hydrogens do not (18 versus 14 + 6 = 20), so the proposal fails the ledger - a correct split must give one alkene, such as C8H18 -> C6H14 + C2H4.

glossary.definition: The separation of crude oil into boiling-point fractions up a temperature-graded column.
Converting straight-chain alkanes into branched and cyclic isomers with better burning properties.
Splitting long-chain alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes with heat and a catalyst.

workedExample.prompt: Crack decane (C10H22) into octane (C8H18) and one alkene. Identify the alkene and verify the balance.
steps: Reserve the saturated product: octane C8H18 takes 8 carbons.
The remaining carbons are 10 - 8 = 2, and they must carry the double bond: C2H4, ethene.
Check carbons: 8 + 2 = 10 - the carbon ledger closes.
Check hydrogens: 18 + 4 = 22 - the hydrogen ledger closes.
workedExample.finalAnswer: C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4, with ethene as the alkene; both ledgers balance.
